extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing creative writers (memoirists, short-story writers) and creative-writing students/workshop participants
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft and ethical guidance for writing and revising short fiction and memoir — covering truthfulness, revision habits, use of experience, workshop practice, and decisions about voice and form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness in memoir
rubrics_metrics.description: Be truthful in memoir; expose other people only if you are equally objective about your own part in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff emphasizes that memoir is about being truthful, not merely convincing readers. If you put other people under a close lens you must put that lens on yourself as well, otherwise the story will be distorted (e.g., making yourself an angel above a fallen world). Balance fairness to others with candor about your own participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid performative confession
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on exaggerated nastiness or confessional affectation as proof of honesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many memoirs overuse the tactic of emphasizing the author's worst traits as shorthand for honesty (e.g., 'I’m such a good person that I’ll tell you how bad I used to be'). This can become a mannerism; don't manufacture contrition as a fashion of candor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memoir requires intersection with other lives
rubrics_metrics.description: Memoir is strongest where the author's life intersects with other people's lives; solitary lives are less likely to make compelling memoir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff notes that 'wherever our lives are interesting is where they intersect with other lives.' If your life is mostly solitary it may not yield a compelling memoir because you lack those interpersonal dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful exposure of others (ethical consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that exposing other people in memoir will have consequences — they may resent your portrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People generally want to control their own narratives. When you write about others in ways they won't like, you must be careful and consider fairness; they won't be grateful for being made public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance tone and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone and motive shape the final form and feeling of a memoir or story; achieving balance is crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff stresses that balance (tone, motive) affects the piece's ultimate shape. Overemphasizing one motive (e.g., self-justification) will alter readers' perception of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise constantly
rubrics_metrics.description: Revision is ongoing — while drafting, at proof stage, when anthologizing, and across editions; view texts as revisable rather than sacred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff revises continuously and even revisits previously published stories. He describes the pursuit of a 'perfect' story and cites examples (Frank O'Connor tweaking final lines) to show worthwhile small changes. Texts are not sacred; improve them whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a split writer/editor identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be both an open, free-writing self during composition and a cold-eyed editor during revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must allow a free spirit to create without crippling self-criticism, then switch to a critical editor who 'considers every sentence guilty until proven innocent.' This split is necessary to avoid paralysis while ensuring rigorous revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider every sentence guilty until proven innocent
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt an editorial mindset that scrutinizes each sentence for faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff recommends treating every sentence as suspect in editing — hunt for vagueness, fat, lack of clarity — and be willing to excise or rework sentences until they earn their place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use workshop and editorial feedback selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops are for learning to accept advice and to reject it; develop the instinct to discern which feedback serves your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of a workshop is not just to accept suggestions but to cultivate the confidence to reject ones that don't fit your aims. Wolff advises testing advice against your intentions and 'the song you’re trying to sing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop independence from critics and reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on reviews or critical opinion as a definitive guide to your work's value or direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff quotes Hemingway — if you believe praise you must accept criticism — and warns that reviews can be contradictory and unhelpful for guiding craft. Use them sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign moral responsibility through character agency
rubrics_metrics.description: In fiction, avoid using external causes (e.g., alcohol) as a moral excuse; show characters' agency so responsibility lies with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff removed booze from a story because alcohol can abdicate human agency; he wanted characters to make bad decisions themselves so the story puts moral responsibility on them rather than on the writer or on a scapegoat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce dramatis personae to sharpen focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the number of characters to better reveal troubled relationships and make dynamics more vivid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff reduced character count in 'Hunters in the Snow' to get down into the strange, troubled relationships (bullying, pain, secrecy) that he wanted to dramatize more vividly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the author's hand off the scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid authorial signals that push readers toward a preferred moral judgment; let the characters and situation create the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff intentionally avoided tipping the reader to his attitude toward the characters, choosing to let their choices and actions speak rather than authorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal experience as raw material, invent when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw on lived experience for texture and atmospherics, but invent events as needed to make a coherent story; if you invent, call it fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff says he invented many crucial events for Old School because 'what happened to me there wasn’t really a story.' He stresses honesty about genre labeling: if you invent you should call it a novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not falsify memoirs (ethical prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate fabrication in memoir is harmful and pernicious, especially when it involves serious historical events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff condemns false memoirs (citing James Frey and others) and emphasizes the broader harm such falsifications do (e.g., enabling Holocaust denial). Ethical accuracy is a responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground scenes in sensory atmospherics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concrete sensory detail (weather, bodily feeling, sounds) drawn from experience to create vivid scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff describes composing atmospherics — weather, the feeling of running down a hill, rage, helplessness — out of personal experience to make scenes convincing and evocative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show work only when it feels finished to you
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring a piece as far as you can and only then show it to a few readers to identify insufficiencies or overdevelopment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff waits until he 'brought the work as far along as I possibly can' before showing it. Early exposure risks obvious criticism; use trusted readers to spot under- or over-developed parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist until resolution emerges (don’t show if you know it’s not right)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you know something is not right in a piece and you can't see the solution, continue working privately until the problem resolves rather than showing it prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff 'bashes his head against the wall' and won't show work he already knows is flawed because readers will simply confirm it's not right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a notebook/journal of sensory details and overheard material
rubrics_metrics.description: Record sights, smells, sounds, overheard phrases, and small surface details to draw on later in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff recommends keeping a journal of concrete surface details (not deep thoughts) — things that will be interesting later — although he admits he personally doesn't keep one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let voice emerge from subject and language rather than searching for voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't chase 'finding your voice'; write about subjects that deeply interest you in language suited to the story and voice will emerge as an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff warns that actively 'searching' for voice is unhelpful and frustrating. Instead write what interests you and use the language that feels right for that material; voice follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate an instinctual ear for useful criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Over time develop a 'musical ear' to hear which pieces of feedback align with what you want to do and which do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through practice you'll refine the instinct to separate advice that describes something you weren't trying to do from advice that helps you achieve what you wanted. This makes you better at accepting useful criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and revisit classics for craft and inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustain reading of master writers (Hemingway, Chekhov, Flannery O'Connor, Dickens, Maupassant) to learn craft, remain inspired, and feel the effects of great writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff lists writers who 'still blow him away' and notes that reading classics can produce self-forgetfulness and desire to reach similar effects; teaching certain writers can also renew their impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision layers different 'selves' over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple passes of revision allow different 'selves' — different perspectives and tastes accrued over time — to interact and improve the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencing George Saunders' idea, Wolff agrees that revising repeatedly lets various authorial positions contribute to the work, making it stronger than if written by only one momentary self.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained attention humanizes characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Close, sustained attention to a character, even an unlikeable one, tends to reveal their humanity and can create reader sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff suggests that examining a character closely often makes them human to readers; good craft can make problematic writers or fascist characters still compellingly human on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use editorial collaboration as a testing ground
rubrics_metrics.description: A good editor marks up work, asks probing questions, and helps you 'hold the work up to the light' to test its strengths and faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolff credits his editor and early teachers for severe editing that taught him to see the fat and vagueness in his work. An editor is valuable for testing decisions and forcing clarity.
